How a kettle knows it is done

By Mira Okafor · 14 March 2026

The switch on an electric kettle does not measure the water at all. It waits for steam, which is a different thing, and the difference is the whole trick of the design.

Inside the handle, a small channel carries steam from the top of the chamber down to a strip of two metals bonded together. They expand at different rates, so the strip bends as it warms, and at one temperature it snaps across and breaks the circuit.

This is why a kettle with its lid open never turns itself off: the steam escapes before it can reach the strip, and the element goes on heating an open pot until someone notices, or until the dry-boil cutout, which is another strip, gets its turn.

A thermostat that only knows the water is boiling when the water tells it, in the one language it has.
